query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys, the ability to form a homogeneous, self-healing passive oxide film under corrosive, mechanically disruptive conditions governs their resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy produced with near-equimolar concentrations of elements that include high-passivating components (e.g., Cr and/or Al) and exhibiting a pristine, as-processed microstructure with an intact initial oxide surface layer.
generation.intervention: Expose samples to a combined tribocorrosion (simultaneous wear and corrosion) test in a controlled laboratory environment, while comparing outcomes for samples with an intact passive film versus samples where the film is intentionally suppressed or removed (e.g., via pre-treatment or chemical etching).
generation.conditions: Testing in a standardized corrosive medium (such as a neutral NaCl solution) while applying cyclic mechanical wear via a tribometer at ambient temperature. Conditions should be maintained so that the medium supports oxide formation, but with a parallel test where the film reformation is limited.
generation.structural_mediator: A uniform, self-healing passive oxide film—likely dominated by compounds of Cr and/or Al—that forms at the alloy surface and can rapidly repair after mechanical disruption.
generation.mechanism: The configurational entropy of the high-entropy alloy promotes a dense and chemically homogenized oxide film, which passivates the underlying metal against further corrosive attack. Although mechanical wear disrupts this film, its rapid regeneration prevents deep metal exposure and limits the synergistic degradation (combined wear–corrosion) that typically accelerates material loss.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline sample with a compromised passive film, samples retaining an intact, self-healing film will exhibit lower overall mass loss and reduced formation of corrosion pits under combined wear–corrosion conditions. Furthermore, the degradation in the combined environment will be less severe than the sum of the individual effects of isolated wear or corrosion.
generation.baseline: A high-entropy alloy sample modified or pre-treated to inhibit passive oxide film formation, or samples exposed to either wear or corrosion separately to highlight the synergy in combined degradation.
generation.boundary: This prediction is expected to hold in environments where the electrolytic medium supports the formation and regeneration of the passive film. In severely aggressive environments that chemically dissolve the oxide layer faster than it can regenerate, or in cases where the alloy’s inherent composition does not allow a continuous film, the protective effect would likely fail.
generation.uncertainty: While there is strong plausibility for the role of a self-healing oxide film, the exact quantitative contribution of the film to lowering combined degradation versus other factors (such as bulk mechanical properties or microstructural heterogeneity) is uncertain. It is also unclear how variations in the specific alloying elements might shift the balance between wear and corrosion resistance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples: one set with the naturally formed passive oxide film intact, and another set where the passive film is removed or inhibited (via chemical etching or a controlled pre-treatment). Subject both sets to identical tribocorrosion tests using a tribometer in a NaCl solution. Document the mass loss, pit formation, and passive film reformation over time using methods like microscopy and surface spectroscopies (e.g., XPS).
measurements: Passive film thickness/regeneration (via XPS or electron microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with an intact passive film do not exhibit a significantly lower rate of combined degradation (in terms of mass loss and pit formation) compared with the film-suppressed samples, or if rapid film regeneration does not correlate with improved resistance, then the hypothesis will be falsified.
